title: Combinatorial Approach to Erdős #485
content: **Combinatorial Approach to Erdős #485**: The known proofs of f(k) → ∞ (Schinzel 1987, Schinzel-Zannier 2009) use algebraic height theory — non-constructive analytic machinery. This file asks: is there a purely combinatorial proof via sumset bounds? The approach: support(P²) ⊆ support(P) + support(P), and sumsets satisfy |A+A| ≥ 2|A|-1. If no cancellation occurs, this immediately gives f(k) ≥ 2k-1 → ∞.
mathContext: The **Cauchy-Davenport theorem** (for ℤ/pℤ) and its ℤ variant: for nonempty finite $A \subseteq \mathbb{Z}$, $|A + A| \geq \min(p, 2|A|-1)$. For $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ (no modular wraparound), $|A + A| \geq 2|A| - 1$. The extremal case is arithmetic progressions: $A = \{a, a+d, \ldots, a+(k-1)d\}$ gives $A + A = \{2a, 2a+d, \ldots, 2a+2(k-1)d\}$ with $|A+A| = 2k-1$. Erdős #485 asks: for any $P \in \mathbb{Q}[x]$ with $k$ nonzero terms, must $P^2$ have $\geq k+1$ nonzero terms? The open conjecture: $f(k) \to \infty$.

title: termCount and f(k): Sparse Term Measure
content: **termCount**: The number of nonzero monomials in a polynomial, defined as `P.support.card`. The `noncomputable` keyword is needed because `Polynomial.support` is a Finset computed via a decidability instance. Works for any Semiring R, not just ℚ. The function **f(k)** is defined as `Nat.sInf {termCount (P^2) | P has k terms}` — the minimum number of terms in P² over all k-term polynomials.
mathContext: For $P = a_0 + a_1 x + \cdots + a_n x^n \in R[x]$, `P.support` is the Finset of indices $i$ where $a_i \neq 0$. Thus `termCount P = |\text{supp}(P)|$ counts the sparse representation. For $P = 1 - x^2 - \frac{1}{2}x^4$: `termCount P = 3`. The definition `f(k) = sInf {...}` uses `Nat.sInf` — the infimum of a set of naturals, which equals 0 for empty sets (a technicality that doesn't affect the main results since the set is always nonempty).

title: Cauchy Convolution Formula for P²
content: **coeff_sq_convolution**: The coefficient of P² at n equals the Cauchy convolution: $\sum_{a+b=n} c_a \cdot c_b$ over `Finset.antidiagonal n`. Proved in one line: `rw [sq, Polynomial.coeff_mul]` — the fundamental algebraic identity connecting polynomial multiplication to sumset structure.
mathContext: Lean's `Polynomial.coeff_mul` states `(p * q).coeff n = ∑ i in antidiagonal n, p.coeff i.1 * q.coeff i.2`. For $P^2 = P \cdot P$, this gives the **Cauchy product formula**: $(P^2)_n = \sum_{a+b=n} P_a P_b$. The set `Finset.antidiagonal n = {(a,b) : a + b = n}` has cardinality $n+1$. The cancellation barrier: opposite-sign terms can make the sum zero even when individual summands are nonzero — this is what prevents the naive sumset argument from working for general polynomials.

title: Support Containment: supp(P²) ⊆ supp(P) + supp(P)
content: **support_sq_subset_sumset**: `supp(P²) ⊆ supp(P) + supp(P)`. If $n \in \text{supp}(P^2)$, the convolution sum at $n$ is nonzero, so some term $c_a \cdot c_b \neq 0$ (with $a+b=n$), giving $a, b \in \text{supp}(P)$, so $n \in \text{supp}(P)+\text{supp}(P)$. Proof by contradiction using `Finset.sum_eq_zero`. Also proves **termCount_sq_le_sumset**: `termCount(P²) ≤ |supp(P)+supp(P)|`.

title: Nonneg Coefficients: supp(P²) = supp(P) + supp(P)
content: **support_sq_eq_sumset_of_nonneg**: For nonneg-coefficient P, `supp(P²) = supp(P)+supp(P)`. The `⊆` direction is `support_sq_subset_sumset`. The `⊇` direction: for each $a+b \in A+A$, the convolution sum at $a+b$ contains the positive term $c_a \cdot c_b > 0$ (from `sumset_elem_in_sq_support_of_nonneg`), so $a+b \in \text{supp}(P^2)$. No cancellation occurs when all coefficients are nonneg.
mathContext: The positive step uses `Finset.single_le_sum`: if all summands are $\geq 0$ and one summand is $> 0$, then the sum is $> 0$. Here the summand at $(a,b)$ is $c_a \cdot c_b > 0$ (since $a,b \in \text{supp}(P)$ and all coefficients are nonneg, so they're strictly positive at support elements). The `Finset.mem_antidiagonal.mpr rfl` places $(a,b)$ at position $a+b$ in the antidiagonal. Hypothesis `hP : ∀ i, 0 ≤ P.coeff i` enables the `mul_pos` argument.

title: Sumset Lower Bound and Main Result: f_+(k) ≥ 2k-1
content: **sumset_card_lower_bound**: For nonempty $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$, $|A+A| \geq 2|A|-1$. Proof: constructs two injections $A \to A+A$ — left injection ($a \mapsto \min(A)+a$) and right injection ($a \mapsto a+\max(A)$) — whose images overlap in $\leq 1$ element. By inclusion-exclusion: $|A+A| \geq |\text{image}_L| + |\text{image}_R| - |\text{overlap}| \geq k + k - 1 = 2k-1$. **termCount_sq_nonneg_lower** chains this to: nonneg P with $k$ terms $\Rightarrow$ termCount(P²) $\geq 2k-1$.
mathContext: Injectivity of $a \mapsto \min(A) + a$ is via omega. Intersection bound: if $\min(A) + a_1 = a_2 + \max(A)$, from $a_1 \leq \max(A)$ and $\min(A) \leq a_2$, omega derives $a_1 = \max(A)$ and $a_2 = \min(A)$, so the intersection has $\leq 1$ element. `card_union_add_card_inter` gives $|L \cup R| = |L| + |R| - |L \cap R| \geq 2k-1$. The full chain: `termCount(P²) = |supp(P²)| = |A+A|$ (from equality) $\geq 2k-1$ (from sumset bound). This is the **ℕ analogue of Cauchy-Davenport** — no Fourier analysis needed.

title: Cancellation Barrier: The Open Problem
content: **cancellation_positions_bound**: $|\text{supp}(P)+\text{supp}(P)| \leq k^2$ (image of $k \times k$ pairs under addition). Combined with `termCount_sq_le_sumset`, gives trivial upper bound $\text{termCount}(P^2) \leq k^2$. **termCount_sq_upper** gives `termCount(P²) ≤ k²` directly. The **cancellation barrier**: mixed-sign polynomials can have `termCount(P²)` anywhere in $[0, k^2]$, and whether it can be 0 (or very small) for large $k$ is the core difficulty of Erdős #485.
mathContext: Proof: `rw [sq]; exact Finset.card_image₂_le _ _ _`. `Finset.card_image₂_le` states $|\text{image}_2(f, A, B)| \leq |A| \cdot |B|$. The cancellation example: $P = 1 - x^2 - \frac{1}{2}x^4$ has $A = \{0,2,4\}$, $A+A = \{0,2,4,6,8\}$ ($|A+A| = 5 = 2k-1$), but $(P^2)_4 = c_0 c_4 + c_2^2 + c_4 c_0 = -\frac{1}{2} + 1 - \frac{1}{2} = 0$, so $|\text{supp}(P^2)| < |A+A|$. Schinzel-Zannier prove $f(k) \gg \log k$ — the combinatorial approach would give $f(k) \geq 2k-1$ if cancellation could be controlled.
